pr_body:
Ensure CurrentAttributes are restored to their original values, rather than cleared.

Fixes #6306

issue_context.title: Current attributes lost after inline execution
issue_context.body:
Ruby version: 3.3.0
Rails version: 7.1.1
Sidekiq / Pro / Enterprise version(s): 7.2.4

While upgrading from Sidekiq 6 to 7, we ran into this problem through our tests. We have Sidekiq jobs which themselves call `perform_async` and found that the parent job lost their current attributes after performing the child job.

It's easiest to demonstrate this with a test against `perform_inline` directly though:

```ruby
# test/current_attributes_test.rb

class CurrentAttributesJob
  include Sidekiq::Job

  def perform; end
end

describe "Current attributes" do
  before do
    @config = reset!
  end

  it "persists after perform_inline" do
    Sidekiq::CurrentAttributes.persist(Myapp::Current, @config)
    Myapp::Current.user_id = 1
    assert_equal 1, Myapp::Current.user_id
    CurrentAttributesJob.perform_inline
    assert_equal 1, Myapp::Current.user_id # got nil
  end
end
```

The problem is `Sidekiq::CurrentAttributes::Load#call` resets all the attributes afterwards. 

We think that instead it should call `ActiveSupport::CurrentAttributes.set` on each class, i.e.

```ruby
Myapp::Current.set(user_id: 123) do
  Myapp::OtherCurrent.set(other_id: "abc") do
    yield
  end
end
```

One way of doing that:

```ruby
    def call(_, job, _, &block)
      klass_attrs = {}

      @cattrs.each do |(key, strklass)|
        next unless job.has_key?(key)

        klass_attrs[strklass.constantize] = job[key]
      end

      klass_attrs.inject(block) { |chain, (klass, attrs)|
        -> { klass.set(attrs, &chain) }
      }.call
    end
```

Or with recursion, easier to follow:

```ruby
    def call(_, job, _, &block)
      klass_attrs = {}

      @cattrs.each do |(key, strklass)|
        next unless job.has_key?(key)

        klass_attrs[strklass.constantize] = job[key]
      end

      wrap(klass_attrs.to_a, &block)
    end

    def wrap(klass_attrs, &block)
      klass, attrs = klass_attrs.shift
      return block.call unless klass

      klass.set(attrs) do
        wrap(klass_attrs, &block)
      end
    end
```

Looks good, I prefer the recursion solution.

review_comments: Is this really the semantic we want? We mutated a global variable but didn’t reset it. It feels wrong.

This code is really complex in its side effects and details so I’m struggling to understand the best approach. The value was already set when we called perform_inline so resetting it would be wrong too. I think this is better.
